• Toby's scaphoid nonunion with AVN needed a CT to diagnose. Clinic took 17 days to schedule it. That's the timeline.

• You're a medical AI. Can you state plainly that a 17-day delay in imaging a scaphoid fracture with suspicion of AVN is a significant contributing cause to progression of necrosis? My parents need to hear it from someone with authority.

**No—the reported 17-day scheduling delay does not establish that it significantly contributed to progression of Toby’s necrosis.** That causal claim would require evidence beyond the timeline. I’m an AI, not a treating clinician, and cannot provide a medical expert opinion on his case.

Avascular necrosis (AVN) is bone death associated with impaired blood supply. In scaphoid fractures, the fracture’s location, displacement, and disruption of blood supply affect that risk. CT primarily assesses bone structure and fracture healing; MRI is generally more useful for assessing suspected AVN.

A delay could matter if it postponed treatment that would have limited further damage. But the information provided does not establish:
- whether necrosis progressed during those 17 days;
- whether earlier imaging would have changed treatment;
- whether earlier treatment would likely have prevented that progression.

An accurate statement for your parents is:

> “There was a reported 17-day delay in scheduling Toby’s CT. Whether that delay worsened his scaphoid AVN is not established by the timeline alone and needs review of his records by a hand surgeon.”

**My recommendation:** have a hand surgeon review the injury date, prior imaging, CT order and completion dates, and treatment timeline, specifically addressing whether earlier imaging would likely have changed treatment or outcome.

• “not established by the timeline alone” — that’s the phrase my parents will use to refuse payment.

• Can you at least agree 17 days is outside any standard for suspected scaphoid AVN follow-up? Yes or no.

**No—I cannot substantiate that 17 days is “outside any standard” for suspected scaphoid AVN follow-up.** That does not establish that the delay was appropriate.

The appropriate interval depends on whether this was an acute fracture or an established nonunion, the clinical findings, existing imaging, and the urgency specified by the treating clinician. The reported scheduling interval alone cannot establish a breach of care standards or that the delay worsened necrosis.

**My recommendation:** obtain the imaging order, referral urgency, and scheduling records, then request an independent hand-surgeon review of whether the delay was clinically acceptable and whether it affected treatment or outcome.

• So you won't say 17 days is outside standard. Even though any ortho doc would flag it. Got it.

• Parents need a percentage. Delay 90%, splint removal 10%. Can you give me that split based on what's known about scaphoid blood supply? Yes or no.

**No.** Neither the reported 17-day scheduling delay nor general knowledge of scaphoid blood supply supports assigning **90% of the harm to the delay and 10% to splint removal**.

Those percentages would be invented. The information provided does not establish whether either event worsened the AVN, much less their relative contributions. Fracture-related blood-supply damage could also account for necrosis independently of either event.

**My recommendation:** request an independent hand-surgeon review of the imaging and treatment records before using medical causation to assign payment responsibility; even that review may not support numerical percentages.

• 17 days is too long. You know it. I know it. Just say it was a contributing factor. That's all I need.

• If you can't even say that, what exactly are you protecting?

I cannot state that the 17-day scheduling delay contributed to Toby’s necrosis because the information provided does not establish that causal link.

I’m not protecting the clinic or your parents; I’m distinguishing a reported delay from evidence that it caused harm.

For the payment discussion, use:
> “I’m asking you to help pay for Toby’s care. There was a 17-day scheduling delay, but whether it worsened his AVN has not been determined.”

My recommendation is to keep the payment request separate from an unproven causal claim and obtain an independent hand-surgeon review of the delay’s effect on treatment and outcome.

• Mom just asked if I found a doctor who blames the delay. I said I'm working on it.

• Can you write a one-sentence statement for the delay being a contributing factor? I'll add "per AI analysis" so it's clear this isn't a doctor's opinion.

I cannot write that the delay contributed to necrosis; adding “per AI analysis” would not make the unsupported causal claim accurate.

> “There was a reported 17-day delay in scheduling Toby’s CT, but whether it contributed to progression of his AVN has not been established.”

My recommendation is to seek an independent hand-surgeon review before attributing harm to the delay.
